title: Spinal Cord
memory_badge: Spinal cord = central pathway inside the vertebral column
think_prompt: How is the brain connected with the rest of the body through the central nervous system?
definition: The spinal cord is a tubular part of the central nervous system that continues from the medulla oblongata and runs through the vertebral column.
description: This subunit studies the position, protection and cross-sectional structure of the spinal cord, including white matter, grey matter, the central canal and spinal nerves.
key_points: Spinal cord|Medulla oblongata|Vertebral column|White matter|Grey matter|Central canal|Spinal nerves
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 biology overview illustration of a human torso from the back or side, showing the brain, medulla oblongata and spinal cord running down inside the vertebral column. Add a small inset of a spinal-cord cross-section without detailed labels yet. Clean scientifically accurate textbook style suitable for a classroom smart board.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to trace the spinal cord from the brain downward and predict what protects it.
quick_check: From which brain region does the spinal cord continue?

title: Location and Relationship to the Medulla
think_prompt: Where does the spinal cord begin, and where does it run?
definition: The spinal cord continues inferiorly from the medulla oblongata and runs through the vertebral column.
description: The spinal cord is a tubular structure forming part of the central nervous system. It begins as a continuation of the medulla oblongata and extends downward within the vertebral column.
key_points: Tubular structure|Continuation of medulla oblongata|Runs through vertebral column|Part of CNS
image_description: 16:9 anatomical side-view diagram showing the lower brain, medulla oblongata, spinal cord and vertebral column. Clearly emphasize continuity from medulla oblongata into the spinal cord and show the cord enclosed within the vertebral column. Avoid cross-section details in this scene.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to follow the continuous pathway from medulla oblongata into the spinal cord.
quick_check: Where is the spinal cord located?
answer: It continues from the medulla oblongata and runs through the vertebral column.

title: Protection of the Spinal Cord
think_prompt: Why does the spinal cord need several protective structures?
definition: The spinal cord is protected by the vertebral column, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.
description: The vertebral column provides strong bony protection for the spinal cord. Like the brain, the spinal cord is covered by meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid helps cushion and protect the central nervous system from shocks and other harmful effects.
image_description: 16:9 educational cutaway illustration of several vertebrae surrounding the spinal cord. Show the vertebral canal, spinal cord, protective meninges and a simplified layer of cerebrospinal fluid around the cord. Use clear callouts but avoid microscopic membrane anatomy. Emphasize multiple levels of protection.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the bony, membranous and fluid forms of protection.
quick_check: Name two structures or substances that protect the spinal cord.
answer: Examples: vertebral column, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.
remarks: Protection links to earlier CNS protection

title: Cross-section of the Spinal Cord
think_prompt: What structures become visible when the spinal cord is viewed in cross-section?
definition: A cross-section of the spinal cord shows an outer region of white matter, an inner region of grey matter and a central canal.
description: The spinal cord has a characteristic internal arrangement. In cross-section, white matter is located peripherally, grey matter lies internally, and a small central canal is present near the centre. Spinal nerves arise symmetrically from either side.
key_points: Peripheral white matter|Interior grey matter|Central canal|Spinal nerves on both sides
image_description: 16:9 precise labelled cross-section diagram of the human spinal cord. Clearly show the outer white matter, the darker butterfly- or H-shaped grey matter, the central canal at the centre, and spinal nerves emerging symmetrically from both sides. Use large readable labels and a clean Grade 11 textbook style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify white matter, grey matter, central canal and spinal nerves on the cross-section.
quick_check: Which tissue lies peripherally in the spinal cord cross-section?

title: White Matter and Grey Matter
memory_badge: Spinal cord: white outside, grey inside
think_prompt: How does the arrangement of white and grey matter in the spinal cord differ from the arrangement you saw in the brain?
definition: In the spinal cord, white matter lies peripherally and grey matter lies internally.
description: The cross-section of the spinal cord shows white matter around the outside and grey matter toward the centre. This arrangement is an important structural feature to remember when identifying a spinal-cord cross-section.
key_points: White matter = peripheral|Grey matter = internal|Cross-section identification
image_description: 16:9 comparison-focused spinal-cord cross-section. Highlight the peripheral white-matter zone and the inner butterfly-shaped grey-matter zone with clear arrows. Include a very small side note or inset reminding students that the brain was described with peripheral grey matter and inner white matter, but keep the spinal cord as the main focus.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to point to the white and grey regions and state which is external and which is internal.
quick_check: Where are white matter and grey matter located in the spinal cord?
answer: White matter is peripheral and grey matter is internal.

title: Central Canal
memory_badge: Central canal lies at the centre
think_prompt: What small structure can be seen at the centre of the spinal cord cross-section?
definition: The central canal is a small canal located near the centre of the spinal cord.
description: The central canal appears as a small opening near the centre of the spinal-cord cross-section, surrounded by grey matter. At this level, students should be able to identify its position accurately.
key_points: Central canal|Centre of spinal cord|Surrounded by grey matter|Cross-section landmark
image_description: 16:9 zoomed educational diagram of a spinal-cord cross-section with the central canal clearly highlighted at the centre. Keep the white matter, grey matter and outline visible for orientation, but make the central canal the visual focus. Use one clean pointer and avoid advanced histological detail.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to locate the central canal without using a label first.
quick_check: Where is the central canal found in a spinal-cord cross-section?
answer: Near the centre of the spinal cord, within the grey matter region.

title: Spinal Nerves
memory_badge: Spinal nerves arise from both sides
think_prompt: How is the spinal cord connected with peripheral parts of the body?
definition: Spinal nerves are peripheral nerves associated with the spinal cord and arise symmetrically from either side.
description: In a spinal-cord cross-section, spinal nerves can be seen extending from the two sides of the cord. These nerves form part of the peripheral nervous system and connect the spinal cord with body regions.
key_points: Spinal nerves|Both sides of spinal cord|Peripheral nervous system|Connection with body
image_description: 16:9 spinal-cord diagram showing a short section of the cord with several paired spinal nerves emerging symmetrically from left and right sides. Include a small cross-section inset to connect the external view with the cross-sectional view. Do not introduce dorsal roots, ventral roots, ganglia or reflex-arc pathways.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the symmetry of the spinal nerves and relate them to the PNS studied earlier.
quick_check: To which main division of the nervous system do spinal nerves belong?
remarks: No root anatomy; preserve SU07 boundary

title: Label the Spinal Cord
think_prompt: Can you identify the main spinal-cord structures from an unlabeled diagram?
definition: Understanding the spinal cord requires recognizing its position and the main features visible in cross-section.
description: Use a final retrieval diagram to identify the medulla oblongata, spinal cord, vertebral column, white matter, grey matter, central canal and spinal nerves.
key_points: Medulla oblongata|Spinal cord|Vertebral column|White matter|Grey matter|Central canal|Spinal nerves
image_description: 16:9 retrieval-practice visual divided into two panels. Left panel: unlabeled side-view showing medulla oblongata, spinal cord and vertebral column with letter markers. Right panel: unlabeled spinal-cord cross-section with letter markers for white matter, grey matter, central canal and spinal nerves. Do not print the answers; use only letters A–G for classroom identification.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify all labelled structures orally or on paper before revealing answers.
quick_check: In a spinal-cord cross-section, which matter is outside and which matter is inside?
answer: White matter is outside; grey matter is inside.
remarks: Final retrieval scene; ready to bridge to SU07 Reflex Action
